text: — I also had a meeting with Bay Ganyo — Kolyo chimed in — in Dresden. — Would you like me to tell you about it?
— Is that even a question? Tell us! — the whole company shouted.

— I do not know whether you have heard — a few years ago the Dresden society was disturbed by an extremely sad catastrophe, the victim of which was a Bulgarian girl, a student, and a young American. I will remind you of this sad incident in a few words. The Bulgarian girl was studying in Dresden. In that city, as you know, there are entire quarters of English, Americans, Russians, and other foreigners, whose children attend the local schools. An American girl, a student, became friends with our Bulgarian girl. English and American schoolgirls have this whim — to take under their protection some schoolmate from among the most defenseless. Such a one had our Bulgarian girl proved to be: a little more timid, a little more humble, a little more silent. They became friends, and the American girl began inviting her to her home on holidays. The Bulgarian girl became acquainted with the whole family, and among the others with her brother, a young man of twenty, who was studying painting. Who knows whether it was due to the tendency, characteristic of young artists, to be carried away by any living model, unsuitable to the general type of the models around them, or due to the Americans’ innate inclination toward originality, but after several meetings with our modest and shy Bulgarian girl, the young man seemed to begin to feel an attraction toward her; he took advantage of every opportunity to meet her, to share his artistic impressions, to be gallant; in a word, they began to love each other. And this love shortened their days.

One holiday day during the summer vacation the whole family, accompanied by the Bulgarian woman, sets out for a walk in Saxon Switzerland. At a rocky picturesque spot the young artist, absorbed in conversation with the Bulgarian woman, had wandered away from the company. A high cliff attracted the young man’s attention, and he began to climb it. His companion follows after him: but they do not manage to reach even the middle of the dangerous cliff, the American slips, and in his fall drags the Bulgarian woman down into the abyss. Thus far their lives had gone.

The dead couple were brought to Dresden, to the clinic. The whole city was distressed by this sad event. A great many people went to see them, laid side by side on a large marble table. At once they telegraphed to the Bulgarian woman’s brother to come to Dresden; she had no closer relatives. The bodies were embalmed in order to preserve them until his arrival. Numerous wreaths adorned their deathbed. On the third day a telegram was received from Vienna saying that the deceased woman’s brother was setting out for Dresden. The bodies were taken to the home of the American family. As they awaited the brother’s arrival with impatience, a great many misters and mistresses, a great many ladies and gentlemen had gathered in that house. The family belonged to Dresden’s high society. I had gone there too, together with several Bulgarian students. We had invitations as Bulgarians, you know, the deceased Bulgarian woman. Others of our little Bulgarians had gone to the station to meet the deceased woman’s brother. We waited. A mournful solemnity! All the apartments were full of visitors. They spoke quietly, in whispers. The silence was broken from time to time by the bitter sobs and desperate sighs of the mother of the deceased young man, broken by grief. In one interval of dead silence, from the corridor there was heard a terrible clamor: rough footsteps were heard — as if they were leading a shod horse — voices were heard: “Where is he? Was he here?” “Shh!... More quietly!” And into the room of the deceased, with a cap on his head... Bay Ganyo slipped in.
— Good day! — he cried out in a tone and with an expression on his face that looked less like sorrow than indignation; as though the surrounding faces were to blame for his sister’s death.

Bay Ganyo approached the deathbed and accidentally pulled back the shroud from the young man’s face. — Who is this? What kind of man is this? — he asked, looking over the whole gathering almost fiercely and waiting for an answer with his eyes fixed intently.

A student, a Bulgarian, overwhelmed with shame, approached Bay Ganyo, gently tugged his sleeve, and pulled the shroud away from the face of the deceased woman. Bay Ganyo took off his cap, crossed himself, and kissed her on the forehead.

— Oh, the poor thing! What was written for her... Mariyke, Mariyke! — Bay Ganyo shook his head. Say what you will, but that head-shaking still looked more like a threat to the visitors than an expression of grief.

He looked suspiciously at the corpse lying next to his sister and, after moving his head and the fingers of his left hand questioningly in an Eastern manner, turned to the student:

— But what is this all about? Why have they put that fellow here? What is a man doing in the boarding house?
— Shh! Please, Mr. Ganyo, speak more softly.
— Why take it easy? I’m spending money here! Where is the director?
— This is not the boarding house; this is a private house — replies the thunderstruck student.
— As a private house?
— Shh... For God’s sake, speak more quietly! — pleaded the unfortunate student, deafened by the blood that had surged into his head, ready to burst into tears.

Regardless of Bay Ganyo’s swaggering behavior and manners, which had already come to resemble blasphemy, a mockery of the sacred feelings of everyone around him, his very appearance also by no means inspired sympathy in the Americans and the English, and especially in their gentler half.

Bay Ganyo was dressed in light-brown homespun clothes, with unclean, dust-covered boots, his neck tied with a large mourning scarf, beneath which could be seen a rather dirty shirt, unbuttoned in the middle. In his hand he held a cane and under his arm a package wrapped in yellow paper. His mustaches were once again curled, and his little beard was once again unshaven—overgrown.
— Is this gentleman the brother of mademoiselle Marie? — one of the household asked me.

I answered him in the affirmative, adding, in justification of Bay Ganyo’s behavior and appearance, a hastily concocted lie: I told him that the telegram with the sorrowful news had found Bay Ganyo on his estate, while he was overseeing his field work, and that, without stopping by his villa (Bay Ganyo and a villa!), he had gone to the railway, obtained money from acquaintances at the station, and come to Dresden without stopping anywhere. And his present behavior, though it may seem strange, ought to be forgiven, considering the overwhelming impression made on him by the irreplaceable loss of his sister and... the enormous losses he is suffering from the untimely abandonment of his field work.
— Oh, the poor man! — my interlocutor said sympathetically and went off to share his feelings about Bay Ganyo with the other household members and friends.

My heart felt lighter, gentlemen! But only for a very short time did it feel lighter. The American, the one from the household, had already managed to communicate the information I had gathered to a large part of those present; their noble indignation, aroused by Bay Ganyo’s manners, had subsided, and everyone looked at Bay Ganyo not only benevolently, but even sympathetically: a terrible telegram that had arrived unexpectedly, an unprepared departure on a long journey, enormous losses — these are such surprises that can stun any person. And with these surprises they indulgently excused Bay Ganyo. But, gentlemen, please tell me, with what could we, the Bulgarian students, excuse the following action of Bay Ganyo. The student who was hovering around him, in order to restrain the impulse of his feelings, was quietly telling him how the catastrophe in the rocks of Saxon Switzerland had happened. During this story Bay Ganyo expressed, with various movements, with his head and hands, the feelings that stirred him: now he would click his tongue and let out, “Tsk, if only it hadn’t been seen at all!”, now he would look at his sister and shake his head: “the poor thing!”, now he would look at the deceased young man, shake his head threateningly and flash lightning from his eyes, as if he wanted to say: “At the very least, that lout has eaten some... some soup.” The foreigners interpreted these grimaces in their own way and hardly guessed their meaning, because otherwise they would not have looked so sympathetically at Bay Ganyo, whom they considered to be distraught with grief. At one point Bay Ganyo, under the impression of the story, clicked his tongue so loudly that everyone turned their eyes toward him. It was precisely at that moment that he placed the thumb of his right hand against the right nostril of his nose, twisted his eyes and mouth a little to the right, lowered his head slightly, and blew through the left nostril of his nose... Then he placed the left thumb against the other nostril, and crackled once more... We were utterly ruined...

You might excuse even that, you will say, because of the haste with which he left: he forgot, you will say, the unfortunate man, in his hurry and confusion, even to take a handkerchief. But that is not so! It is not, because immediately after this operation Bay Ganyo unfolded the package with the yellow book, took out — what do you think? — a whole dozen handkerchiefs and began handing them out to those present, chiefly to the Bulgarians, for “God rest his soul,” repeating as he gave them: “Here, take one too, and say God rest his soul”; or he would beckon to someone with his hand to come closer and shout: “Hey, boy, come here, here’s one for you too, come on, and say God rest his soul   M a r i y k a”...

— I won’t tell you any more, gentlemen — cried Kolyo in despair — you yourselves must try to imagine the faces of the Englishmen and Americans who surrounded Bay Ganyo. I will only tell you that after the funeral service for the deceased was completed in the Russian church as for an Orthodox Christian, and after we buried her, Bay Ganyo was invited to stay, until his departure from Dresden, at the Americans’ house. He spent only one night there. What behavior he kept in that house — I do not know. Only on leaving did he say to the Bulgarian student who was seeing him off to the station:

— Leave it, brother, I was just about to make a mess. I don’t know the ways of these Americans: food everywhere, free of charge, and I ate, ate, I was about to burst from eating; and then at night... Leave it!... But that’s not all, there was another mess: in the morning, you understand, a woman comes, knocks on the door. I — “Come in!” She enters, brings me coffee with milk and various sweets. She sets, you understand, the tray on the table, and then starts sniffing the air with her nose.

— Damn it! Whether she smelled the rose oil or something else! — I, you know, am not a fool, I get up at once, take the perfume bottle and stick it under her nose. She smiled a little. I look at her — a hussy! Dressed so plainly, I thought, a maid. I gave her a look — she laughs! And I — hop! — around the waist. But then she turned around, the devil take her, and gave me such a slap in the face... leave it, I sank!... She turned out to be the boy’s aunt... Well then, good luck to her, the matter ended with one slap. Good people!...
